standard.title: Subitising to 5
standard.description: recognise and name the number of objects within a collection up to 5 using subitising
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can count small collections of objects using one-to-one correspondence. They have not yet recognised quantities instantly without counting — subitising as a deliberate strategy is new.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise and name the number of objects within a collection up to 5 using subitising, without counting.

nodes.label: Instant recognition to 3
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise and name collections of 1, 2 and 3 objects instantly, without counting.
nodes.minimum_width: Recognise collections of 1, 2 and 3 objects instantly in standard arrangements (e.g. dot cards, dice) and name the quantity without counting.
nodes.typical_width: Recognise and name collections of 1, 2 and 3 in a range of arrangements (different dot card layouts, small groups of objects); use subitising to identify quantities in quick-look games.
wider: Recognise collections of 1, 2 and 3 in non-standard arrangements and in familiar objects (e.g. 3 buttons on a shirt, 2 eyes)
Compare two collections of 1–3 objects using subitising — stating which has more without counting

response_modes.reason: Instant recognition requires fluency built through repeated exposure to quick-look activities. Students need practice with many examples across arrangements to build reliable perceptual number sense for 1–3 before extending to 4 and 5.

nodes.hinge_reason: Reliable instant recognition of 1–3 is the perceptual base for extending subitising to 4 and 5 in node 2. Students who count rather than subitise for 1–3 do not develop the perceptual number sense needed to see 4 as '3 and 1 more' or 5 as '3 and 2' — structured subitising at node 2 depends on fluency at this node.
success_criteria: Student names a collection of 1, 2 or 3 objects immediately (without counting) on at least three consecutive occasions
Student can distinguish a subitised response from a counted response ('I just knew' vs 'I counted')

nodes.label: Extending subitising to 5
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise and name collections of 4 and 5 objects using subitising.
nodes.minimum_width: Recognise collections of 4 and 5 objects instantly in standard arrangements (e.g. dice patterns, dot cards) and name the quantity without counting.
nodes.typical_width: Recognise and name collections up to 5 using subitising across a range of arrangements; use subitising to play card games requiring quick recognition of quantities; compare and order collections up to 5 using subitising.
wider: Use subitising to play instructive card games (e.g. memory games with dot cards in different arrangements) — connecting subitising to game contexts
Investigate structured subitising for 4 and 5 as part-part combinations (e.g. 5 as 4+1, 3+2) — beginning to connect subitising to part-part-whole thinking
Explore subitising in everyday contexts — dice, dominoes, tally marks — describing the strategy used

response_modes.reason: Students commonly subitise familiar standard arrangements (dice patterns) but revert to counting for unfamiliar arrangements of 4 and 5. Encountering 4 and 5 in varied spatial arrangements — not just canonical dice patterns — builds flexible perceptual recognition rather than pattern memorisation.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Connecting subitising of 4 and 5 to part-part combinations (structured subitising) is rich territory that bridges to AC9MFN04. Advancing students who can reliably subitise to 5 can begin to see quantities as composed of parts — a genuinely deeper engagement with number.
success_criteria: Student correctly names collections of 4 and 5 objects without counting, across at least two different arrangements
Student uses subitising in a quick-look game context, naming quantities up to 5 immediately
